en: The Questions of King Milinda, Chapter on Mindfulness, 6. The Question on Foul Things as Medicine and Non-Medicine “Venerable sir,” asked King Milinda, “it has been said by the Blessed One: ‘Monks, this body is to be regarded as foul. Yet again, it has been said: ‘Monks, this body is to be used as medicine. Now, how is this? Is it that the body is both foul and not foul? “It is so, great king,” replied the Venerable Nāgasena. “It is both foul and not foul. “But how so, venerable sir? Tell me the reason for this. “The body, great king, is foul by its very nature, but it is not foul when used as medicine. For example, great king, a certain man might have a boil on his head. He would go to a surgeon and say: ‘Good sir, please cut open this boil on my head and extract the pus. The surgeon, having agreed, would cut open the boil with a lancet, wash it with salt water, and apply a medicinal ointment. Would that man feel pleasure from the cutting, the washing, or the application of the ointment? “No, venerable sir. “But why not? “Because the pain, venerable sir, is too great. “In the same way, great king, the body is foul by its very nature, but it is not foul when used as medicine. For what reason? Because, great king, the body is the basis for the cultivation of the seven factors of enlightenment. Just as a man with a head-boil requires a surgeon, so too, great king, one who desires to cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment must attend to the body as medicine. Therefore, great king, the body is foul by its very nature, but it is not foul when used as medicine. “It is wonderful, venerable Nāgasena! It is marvelous, venerable Nāgasena! Well explained is the meaning of what was spoken by the Blessed One in brief: ‘Monks, this body is to be regarded as foul; monks, this body is to be used as medicine.’”

“Venerable Nāgasena, of these two who weep—one who weeps for a deceased mother and one who weeps out of love for the Dhamma—for which of those two weeping ones is the tears medicine, and for which is it not medicine?
“Of the one, O Great King, the tears are stained by lust, hatred, and delusion, and are warm; of the other, they are stainless and cool through joy and gladness.”
“Whatever is cool, Great King, that is medicine; whatever is hot, that is not medicine.
The sixth dilemma: On Tears as Medicine and Non-Medicine.
